MM inventory shocks on HYPE: the story so far

What we have seen, in five threads, and what we think it adds up to. Ten top-volume HYPE market makers (MMs), 2025-03-27 to 2026-06-30, 181 sudden inventory shocks, measured against every wallet labelled a HYPE MM on the day. Every number here is in the full report; figure and table numbers are the report's, so a number here points at the same panel there. Numbers marked record only are in analysis.md and not yet in the report.

Shocks181 (125 up, 56 down)
Rate5.66 per 100 active wallet-days
Detected on10 roster MMs (9 have shocks)
Compared againstmedian 95 active MMs per shock
Quoting measured onall 181, order stream, 1-minute grain
Equity covered138 of 181 shocks, ~2 h snapshots
Evidence typeDescriptive, not causal
Updated2026-09-04

The story in one paragraph

A shock is a one-sided burst of taker flow that lands on the resting quotes of many market makers at once. Every live desk leans the same way; a few end up shocked because they were filled beyond what they could re-quote around. Within minutes they back the accumulating side off the touch and lean the unwind side in, keeping depth roughly balanced, and then work the position out passively over hours. Whether this costs equity does not depend on the inventory itself. It depends on whether the price kept moving against the position and on whether the burst was concentrated on a few desks rather than spread across the market. Systemic shocks are price events shared by everyone and are individually mild; the dangerous ones are concentrated bursts where the shocked desk was run over rather than positioned.

This is a candidate story. Section 7 lists the six tests that would confirm or break it, each with the two competing plain readings and the quantity that separates them.

A. AnatomyThe surge starts before the build, is one-sided in two thirds of shocks, and is absorbed by ~71 desks. The shocked one is the biggest mover, not the biggest absorber.
B. Getting outSlow and passive. The book response is a re-pricing of the accumulating side, not a withdrawal of depth. Speed is set by the desk and by volatility, not by how much it absorbed.
C. Who is hitEveryone leans, a minority is shocked. Systemic shocks are price events; equity damage is monotone in how concentrated the population's move was.
D. EquityThe typical shock does not dent equity. A fifth lose more than 1%, half of that tail is one day. Down shocks hurt twice as often as up shocks.
E. Desks differ more than shocks doBook size and deviation half-life predict reversion; post-only versus crossing is a second axis. Two wallets hold 99 of 181 shocks.
What it does not establishNo causality; ten detected wallets; ~2-hour equity snapshots; 2025-10-10 is its own regime. Section 8.

Thread A. Anatomy of a shock, in time order

  1. The taker surge starts before the build. The first minute where taker flow on the hitting side reaches 3× its baseline precedes the fill-dated formation start by a median 13 minutes (§G).
  2. It is one-sided, and it is not forced flow. Hit-side taker volume runs 5.3× its 24-hour rate during formation (Table 10); taker imbalance goes from +0.01 to +0.44. Over all 181 shocks, 64% are a one-sided hit at a median 11× the trailing 6-hour rate while the other side runs 2.5×; liquidation and ADL volume is zero at the median record only, §20.
  3. The price moves against the inventory being built. The mid fell in 115 of 125 up shocks and rose in 40 of 56 down shocks; median formation move −85 bps, about −$0.30 per HYPE (§F). Inventory z and price z are uncorrelated in size (Spearman 0.00), yet 54% of formations hold a ≥3σ price move.
  4. Many desks absorb it. A median 71 of 95 active MMs take some of the burst, with an effective number of 11 and the top five holding 55% (§D). The shocked wallet is rank 2–3 with 9–11% of hit-side maker volume, but it is the largest standardised inventory mover in 40% of shocks and in the top three in 69% record only, §19.
  5. Much of it is handed straight back. By the peak, absorbers have already sold 43 of every 100 HYPE they bought (Table 14). Retention is bimodal: a quarter of absorbing wallets are flat again by the peak, over a third have sold none, and the largest takes keep the least (82 → 44 per 100 across size quintiles, Table 15).
  6. Takers sell into MMs twice as often as they buy: 125 up shocks against 56 down.

Thread B. Getting out

  1. Slow and often incomplete. Aligned on its own peak, the median shocked MM still carries 38% of its excursion six hours later; only 61% ever get three quarters back; the p75 path sits at 1.00 for the full six hours, so a quarter simply keep the position (Table 16). Shocked MMs outside the ten are slower still (median 0.56 at six hours).
  2. Passive by method. The roster unwinds with post-only orders (98% of volume at the median), never with a TWAP or a frontend market order; two desks are exceptions and cross the spread (rank 7 for 77% of its unwind volume, rank 5 for 23%) (§E2). Post-only unwinding is a property of these ten, not of shocked MMs generally: non-roster shocked MMs that trade the reducing side cross for 20% of it.
  3. The book response is a re-pricing, not a withdrawal. On all 181 shocks, from the two hours before the build to the 30 minutes after the peak, the accumulating-side best quote backs off by 1.36 bps in 81% of shocks while the unwind-side best moves 0.19 bps closer, so the asymmetry widens by 2.07 bps in 80% of 176 (Table 22). Depth on the accumulating side falls to 0.90 of its pre level; the desk never goes dark and never joins the touch. The tilt is already visible during the build and is down to a quarter by the second hour.
  4. The four predicted signs (Table 23): post more at the unwind touch confirms (70% of 180); withdraw more from the accumulating touch comes out opposite, because these desks re-quote every ~1.3 s so cancels travel with posts; post less away from the market fails at 25, 50 and 100 bps; withdrawal away ≥ 0 confirms.
  5. Reaction takes minutes, refill takes one. From surge onset to the first book move: median 9 min, p25 3, p75 23, per-wallet medians 2.5 to 11 min, unrelated to shock size. The accumulating side is back to 80% of its baseline depth within 30 minutes in 87% of shocks, with a conditional median of one minute.
  6. What sets the speed record only, §18: wallet identity alone explains 46% of the variance of log time-to-back; shock size and market volatility add to it; the wallet's absorption share adds nothing once size is controlled. Doubling volatility multiplies time to back by 0.65: faster markets clear the position faster.
  7. Execution against peers is a coin flip. Benchmarked against every MM trading the same side in the same hour off the same reference price, the shocked MM sits at the 46th to 49th percentile on price and markouts (Table 18). The one cell that stands out is the 30-minute markout on down shocks (36th percentile, n = 56).

Thread C. Who is hit: idiosyncratic or systemic

  1. Everyone leans, a minority is hit. Peer direction agreement is near total (median 0.996), yet only 14–23% of active MMs are shocked at a 3σ bar in the three detailed episodes (§D1).
  2. The roster-based classes split into thirds: ALONE 60, FEW 64, BROAD 56 (Table 13). BROAD shocks are the smallest per wallet, come with the largest taker surge and clear fastest. They are price events: 75% of BROAD formations hold a ≥3σ price move against 32% of ALONE ones (§F).
  3. Measured against the market, the roster classes do not survive record only, §19. Against a median 78 active MMs the shocked wallet's share of standardised movement has a median of 0.073, so the ALONE cutoff (≥ 0.60) is reached by 3 of 181 shocks. Read as a concentration curve instead (top-5 share terciles), the equity gradient becomes monotone: 34.8 / 21.4 / 6.0% of shocks lose more than 1% of equity from the most to the least concentrated tercile, and the report's “FEW is worst” disappears.
  4. The worst cell is neither alone nor broad. It is the eight shocks where the population's move concentrated on a few desks and the shocked wallet was not among the top three movers: 5 of 8 lose more than 1%, 3 of 8 more than 5%, median taker surge 28×. Eight shocks, three of them on 2025-10-10: a test to run, not a finding.

Thread D. Equity and constraint

  1. The typical shock does not dent equity. Median change from the last snapshot before the build to the first after the peak is +0.03% (n = 138); equity falls in about 48% of shocks (Table 5).
  2. The tail is real and thin. 20.3% of covered shocks lose more than 1%, 7.2% more than 5%; without 2025-10-10 those are 17.4% and 4.5% (Table 21). Down shocks, where the MM sold into a rising market, lose more than 1% twice as often as up shocks (31.7% against 15.5%).
  3. Constraint is far from binding. Maintenance margin over equity has a median of 0.025 (liquidation at 1.0) and rises by more than 2 pp in 13% of shocks. Effective leverage inside shock windows is 0.65× against 0.28× at all times, and even the in-shock p75 sits a factor of twelve from the 20× liquidation boundary (Table 4).
  4. Resolution caveat. Snapshots are about two hours apart and cover the whole account, so this is an hours-resolution claim and a change can include other coins and deposits.

Thread E. The desks differ more than the shocks do

  1. Axis 1, state: book size × deviation half-life. Median |position| runs from $4k to $10.1m and the half-life of a deviation from the 6-hour median from 3 to 1,162 minutes; the two move together and predict reversion (Spearman −0.93 with the share half-way back within the hour) (Table 20). Exp5's independent spike-versus-cliff propensity is the same axis on another event set.
  2. Axis 2, action: post-only or crossing. Seven wallets unwind 88–99% post-only; ranks 5 and 7 cross. This is not axis 1 in disguise: rank 7 is the fastest reverter and the biggest crosser. Exposure per dollar of equity tracks it (+0.83).
  3. What lines up with neither: equity change, retention of what was absorbed, and execution against peers. Reaction latency from the order stream is per desk 2.5 to 11 minutes and does not track shock size, so it belongs on the archetype table next.
  4. Concentration of events. Two wallets hold 99 of 181 shocks; three contribute six between them; rank 6 has none because it moves a lot of inventory and never quickly.
Exp5's two families are the same axisSpikes revert, cliffs stay. Ranks 6 and 8 produce zero spikes and 34 cliffs; ranks 2, 7 and 10 produce 54 spikes and one cliff. Which kind a desk produces is a property of the desk. Report Figures 1 and 2 show one page of each family.
Why two cataloguesExp5 puts the outcome in the rule (does it come back?); Exp8 keeps it out and labels it afterwards (revert / partial / step). Exp8 keeps 55% of Exp5's spikes and 19% of its cliffs, mostly because slow builds fail the suddenness rule (report overview).

What would make the story a finding: six tests

Each carries the two competing plain readings, the exact quantity, and which direction supports which reading. Nothing below is run yet except where noted.

TestReading AReading BQuantity, and which way points whereData
H1. Why this desk got shocked Size: it had more resting size on the accumulating side at surge onset than peers. Latency: similar size, but it pulled or backed off later than peers. At surge onset, per roster wallet in the window: accumulating-side depth in touch + near buckets, reaction latency, fill-through and withdrawal rate over the build. Shocked wallet's pre-onset depth >> peers at similar latency → A; longer latency at similar depth → B. Exp9 pair_1m, reaction; peers already stored.
H2. Inventory shock + adverse price = equity shock Mechanical: the equity change is the mark-to-market of the shock inventory times the subsequent price move. Portfolio: the equity change comes from other coins or the account as a whole. Predicted HYPE PnL = amplitude × (mid at the after-peak snapshot − accumulation VWAP) against observed Δequity. Slope near 1, high R² → A; no relation → B. Then the reverse for Miao's equity-shock events: was there an inventory shock in the prior 6 h, and an adverse price move? shock_atlas, agg10 5-min state, per-fill k; one shared event grain with Miao.
H3. Idiosyncratic vs systemic, on the market Systemic = price event, mild for each; idiosyncratic = flow selected this desk, worse. The worst is being outside the concentrated group: run over by a burst a few other desks positioned for. Adopt the two-axis label (population top-5 terciles × focal in top 3); equity Δ, M60, recovery by cell, with and without 2025-10-10. Worst equity in ALONE-like cells → A; in CONC-outside-top-3 → B. population_concentration.csv (built, §19).
H4. Does the quote tilt get the desk out? Desks that tilt distance more get flat faster. Reversion is set by the market coming back; the tilt is cosmetic. Add the paired POST1 − PRE asymmetry to the §18 recovery regression (size, volatility, wallet fixed effect). Positive coefficient with an R² gain → A; none → B. Exp9 windows + recovery_panel.csv.
H5. Archetypes completed with quoting Choice: large slow books do not tilt, do not cross, lose no equity; warehousing by design. Inability: they tilt hard but are not filled on the unwind side; stuck. Per wallet: median latency, median tilt, refill time, unwind-side fill-through, next to reversion, execution percentile and equity Δ. Small tilt + low unwind fill-through + no crossing + flat equity → A; large tilt + low fill-through → B. Exp9 tables joined into archetype_chain.csv.
H6. What the market pays afterwards MMs back off, so spread widens, depth thins and taker cost rises for a while. Liquidity refills within minutes (87% refilled by +30 min), so no lasting cost. 5-minute event study, 2 h after the 181 peaks: quoted spread, top-5 depth, taker realised cost and M5 markout of arrivals, against the 24-hour baseline, split by the population axis. Elevated past +30 min → A; back by +30 min → B. Book states, grouped trades; no new infrastructure.

Order of work

  1. Freeze definitions. One catalogue (181 v2; v3 to the appendix). One class axis (population two-axis; roster C retired). One reversion outcome in the body (share recovered at 60 minutes, uncensored, plus share three quarters back by 6 h). One side convention (SAME / OPP). One reference window (PRE in tables). One surge baseline. Three-episode pilot numbers move to the appendix until rerun on 181.
  2. H1 and H4 on the existing Exp9 build (peers and the tilt term). No new compute.
  3. H2, equity attribution, and send Miao the event grain.
  4. Promote analysis.md §18, §19, §20 into the report, relabel §D3, §F, §E3 (H3, H5).
  5. H6, the market event study.
  6. Rewrite the report as a reader document around threads A–E: one figure per thread, one definitions box, one limits list; pilots and galleries in the appendix.

Full detail, with output tables named per test: plans/plan-2026-09-04-exp8-review-status-story-and-next-experiments.md.

What this does not establish

  • Nothing is causal. A flow burst and an inventory build in the same ten minutes is an association on a five-minute grid.
  • Detection is on ten wallets. Shocks that hit only other MMs are invisible; every population figure is measured inside windows the ten defined. Most shocked MMs in the detailed episodes were outside the ten.
  • Equity is hours-resolution and whole-account; 138 of 181 shocks covered.
  • Two wallets are 99 of 181 shocks, so shocks are not independent draws and the share-with-predicted-sign column is the number to trust over any p-value.
  • The book join is not action-exact: the market's best is stale by a median 0.3 s at order timestamps; bucket-level statements only.
  • 2025-10-10 is a distinct regime (41% forced flow, markouts an order of magnitude larger) and is reported with and without throughout.
  • Slow permanent re-targeting is out of scope by construction; one of the ten does exactly that and registers zero shocks.
